title: Standing Tall When The Smoke Clears

sense.text:
“Happy art thou, O Israel: who is like unto thee, O people saved by the Lord”. This is how we come into this truth: on fire, with great joy and zeal. We got our nationality restored. We found out we ain’t just negroes, we ain’t just Latinos, we ain’t just Indians, we ain’t no savages. We are God’s chosen people, and there is none like us.

The Lord is “the shield of thy help” and “the sword of thy excellency”, and “thine enemies shall be found liars unto thee.” So we came in teaching people on break at work, passing out flyers everywhere, flyers in our back pocket. That is fine and that is great. There is nothing wrong with the joy of the Lord; you are supposed to have it. You are not supposed to come in depressed with a thunderstorm over your head.

But there is a balance in this truth. There is going to be some smoke: pain, suffering and struggle. It is not an if, it is a when, and the whole class is about still standing when the smoke clears.

precepts.why:
“The kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.”

That is how you are supposed to come into the truth: for joy, willing to give up everything for it. Family, friends, all Esau’s holidays and traditions. You find the treasure, and you sell all that you have.

“Then they that gladly received his word were baptized”: baptized with laws and understanding, with the word of God. That is what real baptism is. “And the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.”

They gladly received the word. You are supposed to come in with great joy, ready to help, ready to labour, joining offices, not sitting around watching everybody else work. You are not supposed to be a spectator.

“And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart”. They were of one mind, fitly joined together. Gladness and singleness of heart means no ulterior motives and no secret agendas.

“Praising God, and having favour with all the people. And the Lord added to the church daily such as should be saved.” They had gladness, joy, singleness of heart, and a spirit of community: oneness. You are supposed to come in saying, I’m an Israelite, the kingdom is for me, while the other nations go into slavery.

The Bible is supposed to be sweet to you, as it was sweet in the mouth in Revelation. “Thy words were found, and I did eat them”: we found the truth about God’s word and took it in. A few years ago all we did was watch the videos all day; the neighbours probably thought we were construction workers renovating, from the sound of the chisel breaking the bricks in the intro. We were getting that word into our soul.

“And thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart: for I am called by thy name, O Lord God of hosts.” We found out we are called by God’s name, by the name of the Lord of hosts. So we are supposed to come in with that great zeal and that great joy.

But we must understand there will be struggle, pain and hardship. That is guaranteed. Don’t be deceived thinking this is going to be a cakewalk.

sense.text: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?” That tower is your walk with the Lord: whether or not you are going to be able to finish your path to the kingdom. Can you continue in the spirit of Christ keeping the commandments till you die or the sky cracks?

“Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him, Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish.” All of us in this truth are building. We are putting in bricks.
The king who sits down first and consults “whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand” is counting the cost of war. This truth is war.

“So likewise, whosoever he be of you that forsaketh not all that he hath, he cannot be my disciple.”

So what is Christ doing with this parable? He is giving us examples of the pain, the struggles and the obstacles we are going to face, to make us mentally prepared before whatever happens, so that we don’t get deceived thinking this truth is a cakewalk. It is not. It is war. That is why our leadership in these last days keeps telling us: stock up, prepare for famine, study, pray, apply, endure, hold the line. There will be things that come against you.

precepts.why:
“Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.” The apostles taught us the same thing Christ did.

This verse gets quoted a lot, but keep it in context. Paul had just been stoned, stoned until the people stoning him thought he was dead; his body must have been horrific. If it wasn’t for the spirit of God he would have been dead, but the disciples gathered round him and prayed and he stood back up. Then he went back to the very same places where he was stoned and told the people, we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.

So there is a spectrum. The end of the spectrum, the extreme and the peak of suffering, is persecution: martyrdom, being put to death, thrown in prison. That is what Paul had just suffered. But in this truth you are going to suffer everything in between, from joyfulness and gladness all the way to persecution, and we must be mentally prepared to face it.

This is speaking of how we are going to obtain immortality and eternal life. “The entrance thereof is narrow”: it is not easy, it is a strict walk, “and is set in a dangerous place to fall, like as if there were a fire on the right hand, and on the left a deep water”. We are walking through perilous times. In these last days the most wicked kingdom on earth is ruling the whole earth, and we have sin and lust all around us and within us. Fire on one side and deep water on the other means there is very little margin for error.

“And one only path between them both, even between the fire and the water, so small that there could but one man go there at once.” That means you can’t save nobody but yourself. You have to endure and fight. You can’t ride into the kingdom on anybody else’s coattail. That’s my officer, that’s my counsel of a thousand: but do you listen to the counsel? Do you apply it? You are not getting the kingdom because you have a righteous counsellor of a thousand. You have to apply yourself.

“If this city now were given unto a man for an inheritance, if he never shall pass the danger set before it, how shall he receive this inheritance?” That danger is the suffering, the pain and the tribulation. “Even so also is Israel’s portion.” That is our portion, our plight.

“Because for their sakes I made the world: and when Adam transgressed my statutes, then was decreed that now is done.” Everything was given to Adam; immortality was given to them. But when Adam transgressed, “Then were the entrances of this world made narrow, full of sorrow and travail”. In this truth there will be sorrow and travail. “They are but few and evil”: few and evil days. Full of perils, which is trouble in all its variations, “and very painful.”

“This is the condition of the battle, which man that is born upon the earth shall fight”. The whole Bible is telling you over and over that you have to fight. It’s narrow; it’s fire on one side and deep water on the other; it’s battle; this is war. It tells you over and over to prepare you mentally for what’s to come. All of us are going to fight.

“That, if he be overcome, he shall suffer as thou hast said”: if you get overcome by the sorrow, by your lust, your temptation, your sin, if you faint in the day of persecution, you are going to suffer as God said. “But if he get the victory, he shall receive the thing that I say.” That is the kingdom.

sense.text:
“Yet man is born unto trouble”. Not good days and a permanent honeymoon in this truth. God is telling us over and over that this truth is going to try us and push us to our limits.

A lot of Israel think something strange is happening to them, calling the captain and going ballistic, as if we are not in captivity, as if the devil is not ruling the planet earth, as if we never read Deuteronomy 28 or First Kings. These things were written for our learning.

“As the sparks fly upward.” When you put a log in the fire at night, what happens? The sparks fly. It is bound to happen; it is natural. Just like trouble is natural.

precepts.why:
“Great travail is created for every man”. Not just some of us: every last one of us, man, woman and child. “And an heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam”: a heavy burden is upon us, “from the day that they go out of their mother’s womb, till the day that they return to the mother of all things.”

So we can’t be shocked when these things happen. You have problems in your personal walk? That’s normal. Marital trials? Why are you shocked? What Bible are you reading?

The Lord knows exactly what he is doing. “Wherein ye greatly rejoice, though now for a season, if need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations”. Sometimes, Israel, we are going to be in heaviness.

“That the trial of your faith”: if you have a court case, they can’t just convict the person; there must be a trial to prove the truth of the matter. We say we love the Lord, we want immortality, we want the kingdom. Your life will be tried to see if that is actually the case.

“That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ”. That is what God wants. The fire is that great travail, that pain, that suffering, and it is guaranteed. A lot of Israel think they are going to skate through this truth: come in, find a good wife or a good husband, and live happily ever after. The Bible never said that, nowhere at all.

Once we come into the truth it’s not going to be a smooth ride at all. “For the thing which I greatly feared is come upon me”. Job was keeping God’s laws, but he understood that evil will come: there will be a rainy day and a sunny day. He kept that in the back of his mind. Even though he kept the laws, he knew the Lord can put him in any situation if he pleases.

“I was not in safety, neither had I rest, neither was I quiet; yet trouble came.” He wasn’t comfortable. He knew the Lord can change his circumstances at any time, so he didn’t put his feet up and just chill. Yet trouble came. Trouble will come; that’s it.

This is why Job could say the thing he feared had come upon him. “The righteous, and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God”. Everything we do is in the hands of the Lord.

“All things come alike to all: there is one event to the righteous, and to the wicked; to the good and to the clean, and to the unclean; to him that sacrificeth, and to him that sacrificeth not: as is the good, so is the sinner”. That one event is the perils, the trouble and the tribulations. Even those that sacrifice have things come upon them. We all get it; the Lord said it will come. When you go back to Job with this, it all makes sense. That was a cold precept.

“My son, if thou come to serve the Lord, prepare thy soul for temptation.” My son and my daughter. “Set thy heart aright”: that goes back to what Christ taught in Luke 14 about counting the cost. Mentally prepare.

“And constantly endure”. Read between the lines: why does it say you have to constantly endure? Because you are going to be constantly catching hell. Peter said we will be in heaviness through manifold temptations, and you have to constantly endure those manifold temptations. The whole Bible is preparing you mentally for war, spiritual war, and soon it is going to turn physical: not because we are going to do anything, but because the other nations will come against us, because they fear the resurrection of the nation of Israel.

“And make not haste in time of trouble.” Don’t run, because trouble will come; Job said he wasn’t quiet, yet trouble came. The trials and the temptations are all wired into the walk. You cannot separate your walk in righteousness from your pain, your suffering and your trials.

sense.text:
Our trials and sufferings take place in different forms, and one thing we have to suffer daily is the lust within our own hearts. That in itself is a daily fight and a daily battle. A sister walks by and you develop a sudden case of Parkinson’s: I’m not going to look back. Spiritual correction in the hot seat of the war room is no joke either. But first, the most common thing we have to suffer is our own lust. Our own mind is against us.

“For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other”. That is a constant battle, and it is taking place inside of you.

“So that ye cannot do the things that ye would.” We want to obey God and do the things pleasing to him, but it is a struggle every single day just walking in righteousness, because all your members are looking for instant gratification: the alcohol, fornication, pornography, all right at our fingertips. We have the smartphone and we do dumb stuff with it. Some of y’all need flip phones.

precepts.why:
One of the major problems is right there in the mirror. It’s you in your own way, you blocking your own blessings. “But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust”. When you were a kid in trouble you said the devil made me do it. That ain’t what the Bible says.

Satan can’t tempt you unless you already like that thing, unless you already partook of it and used to indulge in it. The key word is own. It belongs to you: your own lust that you didn’t kill, didn’t work on, that you entertained, and now it’s got you. “And enticed. Then when lust hath conceived”: you say, you know what, I’m going to go ahead and do that thing. “It bringeth forth sin”: it brings forth the act.

The honeymoon phase wears off. Your old friends reach out to you, your ex sends you that WYD text at 1:40 in the morning. Then you have to apply the Holy Spirit of discipline.

The main common battle is right within ourselves. “But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind”: Paul sees something inside his body warring against the law of his mind, meaning God’s laws and commandments, “and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members.” It is a constant battle within.

“O wretched man that I am!” You walk around thinking you have this thing figured out, that you are holy, that you are righteous. Paul was a chosen vessel unto God, and even the chosen vessel said, “O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?”

This is where the fight starts, right within ourselves. The flesh got smoke for you every day, as soon as you wake up. “For the thoughts of mortal men are miserable”. Don’t trust yourself. “And our devices are but uncertain.” That’s why you have to do what this Bible says, and be around godly men.

“For the corruptible body presseth down the soul”. All of us are dwelling in corruptible bodies; don’t think you already have the celestial body. Before the white man can oppress you, the flesh is oppressing you every single day. “And the earthy tabernacle weigheth down the mind”, this body weighing down the mind that holds God’s laws and commandments, “the mind that museth upon many things”: Cardi B, Megan Thee Stallion, Young Thug, Sexy Red, foolishness and sin. One of the main wars daily is within self.

“Let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us”. That’s a cut right there. As wise as we think we are, sin easily besets us. We have to be ready every single day for the smoke the flesh has for us. We are ready for Clubhouse, but not ready to put the pornography down. We have to wake up understanding, I have to conquer me, I have to bring my body into subjection.

“And let us run with patience the race that is set before us”. Here the truth is called a race, and in Luke Christ called it a tower. A tower needs planning before you build it: that’s counting the cost, self-examination. A race needs endurance and training: that’s studying.

And when we give in to our lust, brothers and sisters, we bring more suffering and more pain into our lives. It’s better to conquer your sin than to give in to it.

sense.text:
“Why criest thou for thine affliction?” Ain’t this how your father sounds after he tears your behind up? You are not allowed to cry in a black house.

“Thy sorrow is incurable for the multitude of thine iniquity: because thy sins were increased”. God says it is because of the multitude of your sin, so stop crying when all hell breaks loose. Sometimes God has to disturb and disrupt our lives so we get a wake-up call.

So we have to examine these things and take some accountability. We always get on sisters about not liking accountability, like it’s kryptonite to them, but brothers don’t like it either. I keep losing my job: maybe you’re not easy to get along with. Maybe you’re in the midst of secret sin, and God has to disrupt your life so you can examine yourself. Watch brothers who had eight jobs in a twelve-month period.

precepts.why:
Sometimes our iniquity brings more suffering into a life that already has suffering planned out for it. “But the way of transgressors is hard.” The way, meaning the life, of transgressors is hard.

Sometimes we make our own lives harder than they have to be, because we are living in secret sin, and then all hell breaks loose: in the marriage, on the job. That’s what be going on.

We have to just take it, and learn the lesson God is trying to teach us. “Wherefore doth a living man complain, a man for the punishment of his sins?” God is asking why y’all complain so much. The reason all hell is breaking loose is that you are getting punished for your own sin. God is looking at you like you’re crazy.

“Therefore now amend your ways and your doings, and obey the voice of the Lord your God; and the Lord will repent him of the evil that he hath pronounced against you.” If you amend your ways and obey, God will repent him of the evil.

Understand: every time you sin, God is pronouncing evil against you. We don’t understand what goes on in that other realm; there are conversations happening while you are in the midst of that wickedness: God is going to bring some evil into your life. And it’s a spectrum. We don’t want no smoke with God. Trust me.

David was a man after God’s own heart, but watch what God did. We know what happened with David and Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite. “Wherefore hast thou despised the commandment of the Lord, to do evil in his sight? thou hast killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword”: you killed your brother, “and hast taken his wife to be thy wife”, and you didn’t even kill him yourself: you put him in the hottest part of the battle and told the soldiers to pull back from him.

“Now therefore the sword shall never depart from thine house”. How long is never? David was at war his whole life, and Solomon had peace forty years because David was at war all that time.

“Behold, I will raise up evil against thee out of thine own house”. The Most High is the king of terrors. He used David’s own sons: one son raped his daughter, another son took the kingdom. “And I will take thy wives before thine eyes, and give them unto thy neighbour”. The Most High is nothing to play with at all.

“For thou didst it secretly: but I will do this thing before all Israel”. The Lord let his son take the kingdom, and David was wandering in the wilderness with his wives for a long time.

sense.text:
When you are in that low period you have brought on yourself, you have to take everything that comes with it. You can’t be heady and high-minded when you are going through affliction you brought upon yourself. The Lord judged David; Absalom took the kingdom in a coup, a conspiracy against David, and David had to flee Jerusalem and wander the wilderness. That was a demotion from the Lord for a period of time.

It’s similar in this truth: demotions happen. If you are in the midst of sin you might lose your rank. Back in the day leadership would snatch your pin and leave a hole in your shirt where your rank used to be. These things are written for our learning today, so let’s check David’s spirit in his demotion. Was he contrite, or was he arrogant?

“Behold, thence came out a man of the family of the house of Saul, whose name was Shimei, the son of Gera: he came forth, and cursed still as he came.”

“And he cast stones at David”. David is on the run, the throne taken by his son, walking with his wives and his mighty men, and now some random Benjamite (shout out to Benjamin) is throwing stones at him, on top of the judgment God raised up in his own house for his sin.

“Come out, come out, thou bloody man, and thou man of Belial”: he is provoking him and calling him the devil. It is crazy what people will do when you are down. But when you are in that low, you have to take all of it. You have to still be standing when the smoke clears.

“The Lord hath returned upon thee all the blood of the house of Saul”. Is that why David was going through this correction? Did David have anything to do with Saul’s death? Hell no. David loved Saul; he would not even touch the Lord’s anointed. “Because thou art a bloody man” was a lie, not why David was in his lowest state.

So you have somebody cursing him, throwing stones, calling him the devil, and accusing him of something he didn’t even do. But when you are on the low you brought upon yourself, take the low road. Take the load. Keep it moving. Stay in the spirit.

Abishai, one of the mighty men, said, “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? let me go over, I pray thee, and take off his head.” Why let this little peon curse at you? Let me take it from him.

“So let him curse, because the Lord hath said unto him, Curse David. Who shall then say, Wherefore hast thou done so?” David was contrite. He was examining himself and reflecting. None of what Shimei said was true, but David said it’s all good, the Lord put that in his spirit, let him curse. David understood that he had brought this affliction upon himself, so whatever came with the lower state he took, because it was good for him.

So when you bring more pain, suffering and affliction into your life, deal with whatever comes with it. Don’t make haste in time of trouble. Don’t bug out, don’t get out of character, don’t get out of the spirit. Be humble, be contrite, learn something, reflect and grow, and still be standing when the smoke clears.

Other times you may say: I’ve been doing good, I’ve been striving in the truth, why is calamity happening to me at work, with my wife? Sometimes it is self-inflicted. Other times it is sudden destruction and sudden loss. Like that cold precept: even the righteous, even he who sacrifices, even when you are striving to do your very best, there are still going to be times of loss.

Look at Job’s resume: “that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil.” He stayed away from evil and didn’t deal with it. Surely we are not better than Job. No book of the Bible says any one of us is perfect and upright. We are of less stature than our fathers in these last days.

“Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth”. There are dialogues in the other realm. Sometimes you bring those conversations on yourself; other times it may just be the Lord God trying your faith.

“Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side?” Those are the good days: the marriage is going good, the finances are in order, your credit went up a couple points, you did your famine prep with your cans organized and dated. You ain’t lucky. God has a hedge about you: wife, children, health, finances.

“But put forth thine hand now, and touch all that he hath, and he will curse thee to thy face.”

“Behold, all that he hath is in thy power; only upon himself put not forth thine hand.” Satan has to get permission. When we go through our trials, our suffering, our pain, there are still limitations. God is not letting Satan have a free-for-all in our lives. There are boundaries, only so far he can go, so we have to exercise our strength in that time, understanding that God won’t put more on us than we are able to overcome.
In one day Job lost a great deal of his wealth, his livestock and his cattle, and his sons were killed when the house fell in on them. “The Sabeans fell upon them, and took them away”.

“Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped”. He didn’t bug out; he worshipped. “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither: the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.”

That’s the level we have to strive to get to. It isn’t written here for nothing, and it isn’t going to be easy. A lot of us would lose our minds if we went through this in one day.

“In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly.” He stayed in the spirit. And after this the Lord allowed Satan to attack his health, and his wife told him to curse God and die. We can’t lose patience; all these things are part of the walk.

precepts.why:
“Prosperity and adversity, life and death, poverty and riches, come of the Lord.” Job was a man that had prosperity, and then adversity. Life and death, and everything in between on the spectrum; poverty and riches, and everything in between, paycheck to paycheck. All of it comes of the Lord.

“Wisdom, knowledge, and understanding of the law, are of the Lord”. In those times of poverty and tribulation, we have to apply the wisdom and knowledge that is also from the Lord. He gives us enough wisdom and knowledge to get through the times of struggle and the lowest states. He gives us everything we need.

sense.text:
Here are more examples of righteous men who had all hell break loose in their lives. We forget these things when we catch hell and say, I’ve been giving my alms, I’ve been travelling, and I keep catching hell. What Bible are we reading? These things are part of the walk.

“Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age: and he made him a coat of many colours.” Shout out to Ephraim and Manasseh. That coat was bad.
“They hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him.” Joseph didn’t do nothing wrong. He had the spirit on him; he had dreams and visions.

“They conspired against him to slay him.” “Behold, this dreamer cometh”: here comes this dang dreamer. “Come now therefore, and let us slay him, and cast him into some pit, and we will say, Some evil beast hath devoured him”. They planned to kill their brother and lie to cover it up.
Reuben said, “Let us not kill him”, and “Shed no blood”.

“And Judah said unto his brethren, What profit is it if we slay our brother, and conceal his blood?” Shout out to Judah. “Come, and let us sell him to the Ishmeelites, and let not our hand be upon him; for he is our brother and our flesh.”

“And the Midianites sold him into Egypt unto Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh’s, and captain of the guard.” He passed through the hands of Ishmael and Midian and ended up in Egypt in the house of Potiphar.

Joseph was the good one. He told on the other brothers, he had dreams, the spirit of God was on him; he was a good son, faithful, honest, with integrity, even rebuking his brothers. And all of a sudden, sudden calamity came upon him unawares.

Now Joseph is in Potiphar’s house. “And Joseph found grace in his sight, and he served him: and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand.” He went from a good estate with his father, in a coat of many colours, with the spirit of God upon him, to being suddenly thrown into a pit, almost put to death and sold into Egypt in a lower state having done no wrong. Now the Lord God put him back in a higher state, with great authority.

“The Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake; and the blessing of the Lord was upon all that he had in the house, and in the field.” Blessing, flourishing: prosperity comes of the Lord. He left everything in Joseph’s hand, and Joseph “was a goodly person, and well favoured.”

“His master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph; and she said, Lie with me. But he refused”. We know how that went on the plantations; we read the books about what the white woman did to us. Joseph said, “how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” He would not sin against God.
“And she caught him by his garment, saying, Lie with me: and he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out.” That is what fleeing from sin as from the face of a serpent looks like.

She called the men of her house and said, “See, he hath brought in an Hebrew unto us to mock us; he came in unto me to lie with me”. That’s how you know this is spiritual Egypt: crying rape is what the white woman always did in the time of slavery. That’s how Rosewood got burned down.

“His wrath was kindled.” Even though Joseph was faithful and would not transgress against his God, “Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, a place where the king’s prisoners were bound: and he was there in the prison.” Back into a lower state, while doing what’s right.

These things were written for our learning. They are not fictional tales; this is the history of our fathers, and we are our fathers. It is a cycle. Affliction is going to happen. Sometimes you bring it upon yourself, and sometimes it comes suddenly while you are doing right and moving in integrity. Trials, suffering and pain are part of the walk.

David fled twice. The second time he brought it upon himself, and the Lord raised up evil in his own house. But did David do anything the first time he fled?

“The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David”: David was in good favour with Jonathan, the king’s son. “And Saul took him that day, and would let him go no more home to his father’s house.” David had great position; Saul said, you stand with me.

“Then Jonathan and David made a covenant”, and “Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was upon him, and gave it to David, and his garments, even to his sword, and to his bow, and to his girdle.” The robe of the king’s son was glorious. That was a great honour.

“And David went out whithersoever Saul sent him, and behaved himself wisely: and Saul set him over the men of war”, like a captain, “and he was accepted in the sight of all the people”. He was in great honour and behaved himself wisely.

When David returned from the slaughter of the Philistine, the women came out of all the cities singing, “Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.” A lot of beefs in the hood go back decades, and if you trace them to the source it’s a woman.

“And Saul was very wroth, and the saying displeased him”, and he said, “what can he have more but the kingdom?” Saul thought David was going to take the kingdom from him. Saul got the devil on him, while David was just behaving himself wisely and being a good servant to Saul.

Saul was brewing and wanted to kill David, but Jonathan stepped in: “Let not the king sin against his servant, against David; because he hath not sinned against thee, and because his works have been to thee-ward very good”. He was reminding his father of the history: David has been doing good, he is in the spirit.

“For he did put his life in his hand, and slew the Philistine, and the Lord wrought a great salvation for all Israel: thou sawest it, and didst rejoice”. Sometimes people will rejoice with you just to make you think they are good with you. The Lord sent David to help Saul, but Saul saw him as competition, as his replacement, and started to envy him. Not every smile has a good heart behind it; some white teeth have a dark heart.

“And Saul sought to smite David even to the wall with the javelin”. That’s attempted murder. David had just put his life on the line against Goliath and delivered Israel; he was a captain warring with our enemies, behaving himself wisely, righteous, in honour with Saul’s son. Why was this happening to him?

Sometimes you will go through suffering and pain that you did not bring upon yourself. But God has a design for everything; everything is designed to build you. “And David fled, and escaped that night.” This was the first time he fled, and he did no wrong.

“So David fled, and escaped, and came to Samuel to Ramah”. Now David is wandering, sleeping in caves: the chosen of the Lord, a man after God’s own heart, fleeing for his life. God allowed him to suffer. How much more us?

“He saw a man which was blind from his birth.” The disciples asked, “Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?” They understood that your actions, or the actions of your parents, can bring evil upon you: in your finances, at your job, in your health.

“Jesus answered, Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him.” Some things are just of the Lord. The Lord has a purpose for everything, and that man’s suffering had nothing to do with sin.

We have to stop moving like Israel does as soon as somebody catches hell: the brother probably has something going on; the sister’s car broke down, she probably did something. The brother got hurt at work: you better repent, it’s going to be worse next time. Charity thinketh no evil, family. The Lord has his own divine purpose and his own will that we are not privy to.

“A woman having an issue of blood twelve years”: a health problem she battled for twelve years. Imagine the pain and sorrow year after year, Passover after Passover, Tabernacles after Tabernacles, Atonement after Atonement: dang, Lord, I thought you forgave me. She “had spent all her living upon physicians”, so her health constraint became a financial constraint too, and she “neither could be healed of any”.

She “touched the border of his garment: and immediately her issue of blood stanched.” “Somebody hath touched me: for I perceive that virtue is gone out of me”: his power. When she saw she was not hid, she came trembling and declared before all the people why she had touched him, “and how she was healed immediately.”

“Daughter, be of good comfort: thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace.” Suffering will show your faith. When you endure your pain, your trial and your suffering, it shows the level of faith you have. God has a purpose behind every situation you might look at as inconvenient, and he deals with us individually and as a nation like that.

precepts.why:
This is the Lord dealing with us as a nation. “Thou shalt remember all the way which the Lord thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart”. He led us in the wilderness forty years, going in circles, lacking bread and water at times, humbling us and proving us so he could see what was in our heart.

You can’t see what’s in a man’s or a woman’s heart when everything is good. You want to know if your wife is really down for you? Wait till y’all fall on hard times; you’ll find out what you married. That’s how you know what’s in somebody’s heart: when they are going through affliction. “Whether thou wouldest keep his commandments, or no.”

“And he humbled thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna”, “that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only”. God wants us to show ourselves faithful whether we are going through prosperity or adversity, and to depend on him at all times, not trusting in uncertain riches or in this present life.

That sister waited twelve years to be healed. Some of us are very impatient in this truth: we call for counsel on a Thursday and call again the same Thursday. You have to apply the understanding for a period of time before you double back.

“The Lord is good unto them that wait for him, to the soul that seeketh him.” You are not alone. Sometimes we think our prayers aren’t being heard. That’s not the case.

Satan has you thinking you’re the only one going through it. Lies: we are all catching all manner of hell, and we are not alone. “They that trust in the Lord shall be as mount Zion, which cannot be removed, but abideth for ever.”

“As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the Lord is round about his people from henceforth even for ever.” We have to remember that. God has a purpose for everything: the pain, the trials, the suffering, the fiery furnace of affliction.

sense.text:
There is no such thing as becoming anything worthwhile without adversity. A man who says that when he has a son he will put as much adversity as possible in his son’s life: what do you think the Father is doing to us?

“The fining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold: but the Lord trieth the hearts.” He tries us by putting us in the pot and in the furnace. The same thing the silver and the gold have to go through, man has to go through, so that God can try our hearts.

precepts.why: “But he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold.” So we have to stop questioning God. We have got very accustomed to questioning God, and we have to stop.

God don’t answer to us; we answer to him. Jeremiah went down to the potter’s house, where clay is made into pottery, “and, behold, he wrought a work on the wheels.” He was forming it with his hands.

“And the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it.” As he was forming it he marred it, then took that marred clay and made it into something better in the end.

“O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the Lord. Behold, as the clay is in the potter’s hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel.” God can mar us at any time, in various ways and manifold temptations, but the end result will be better than it was before. God has divine purpose behind everything.

When you suffer, you learn yourself. Like fight or flight: just as the body reacts to danger, your inner life does the same in trials. Your senses are heightened, your perception is sharpened, and your understanding increases. You hear your inner voice, which is Christ, more distinctly when you are catching hell, and you start to meditate on scriptures you don’t normally think about. You have to know when to stand firm, and when to humble yourself and stay in the spirit like David did when Shimei the Benjamite was throwing stones at him.

If you are sincere, Christ will be strong within you when you are catching hell. Paul was complaining about the thorn in his flesh, and the Lord said, you good: “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” My strength is perfect when you are weak; you are going to overcome.

“Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.” “Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities”: in my trials and my temptations; “in reproaches”: people despising us, painting us as a hate group, defaming and slandering us; “in necessities”: not having enough, paycheck to paycheck, struggling, starving; “in persecutions”: the end of the spectrum, which we all have to prepare for. All these things mould us and prepare us for the end of the rope. “For when I am weak, then am I strong.”

After the trial passes and you overcome it and do what’s right, there is a spiritual recalibration: you recover your balance, take in the new lessons and strength, and become less reactive next time because you have learned resilience.

“It is good for me that I have been afflicted”. After you catch that hell and overcome, you say, dang, I learned a lot from that correction. It didn’t feel good at all, but I learned a lot. Like in Birth of a Nation after he got whooped: you learned your lesson, boy? Oh yes, I’ve learned. That’s how it is in this truth: leaders of correction hit you with them stripes, you get put in the hot seat, maybe a demotion, and you learn your lesson.

“That I might learn thy statutes.” In trials your focus narrows to what matters most, distractions fall away, and clearer values come out. We men in purple live under constant pressure, waking up with the world on our shoulders every day, and after a trial the inner life needs rest and realignment.

sense.text:
After the trial you learn a lot about yourself; you have to realign and refocus. “Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith”. Before a trial, in the middle of it and after it, you have to examine yourself: how did I handle that trial? How did I handle that temptation? Then you can properly and accurately gauge where you are in the spirit.

“Prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?” How we respond to struggles, obstacles, pain and suffering teaches us things about ourselves that we could never learn without the trial. Adversity serves many purposes.

precepts.why:
We all think we know ourselves, but you don’t know yourself when everything is good. That’s why leadership says you don’t know a brother until after he gets corrected. You might not know a sister you are proving until y’all have a disagreement, and her head spins around: it’s time to pull the plug.

“If thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small.” You might think you’re big and bad in this truth, but if you’re going home watching porn every night, if you have a work husband or a work wife, if you faint in these temptations and trials and sufferings, your strength is small. You wouldn’t know your strength was small if it wasn’t for the adversity.

“Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.” Don’t trust yourself. Adversity is the test that shows where your strength is, whether small or great; it’s the deciding factor.

“There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man”: we are all catching it, all going through it. “But God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.” So we can’t faint in these times.

Whether you faint or overcome in these battles, it will show you where you are in the spirit. God already knows; you are not surprising God. He is revealing to you where you are.

“I had fainted, unless I had believed to see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living.” If you faint in adversity your strength is small, but when you have that great faith in you because you are studying, you are not going to faint, because you believe and want to see the Lord. You won’t fall to fornication and adultery, and if you do fall, you’ll get back up and repent, because you believe to see the Lord.

“Wait on the Lord”, like the sister who had the issue of blood twelve years. “Be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart”. These trials are your teachers. You can learn more from a trial than from skimming your four chapters just to check a box. The trial is when you actually exercise what you’ve been learning.

“My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations; Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience.” When you go through suffering over and over, you build up a tolerance for it, you start to understand what’s going on, and you become stronger in the end.

“But let patience have her perfect work”. You get the patience, that tolerance, from the adversity and the suffering. “That ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing.” Before the suffering we are incomplete in many ways in our spiritual walk. After the trial we can apply things we never applied before, and be entire, lacking nothing. The Lord wants us in the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ.

sense.text:
Many times correction is going to come from men, from leadership, from men who bleed just like you, and it ain’t going to feel good. You have to take it and understand it’s for your benefit.

“Let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness: and let him reprove me; it shall be an excellent oil, which shall not break my head”. It is not to break your spirit. The correction you get from men based on God’s word and God’s law is a kindness to you, because you can’t see everything. We have a limited view. The eye sees, but can’t see itself: we can see everything going on but our own selves and where we fall short. So God puts men around us who can see what we can’t.

precepts.why:
God has a remedy for that; that’s what the body is for. It ain’t always going to be sunshine and compliments. Sometimes somebody is going to tell you about yourself so you can fix yourself. That’s real love.

“That which I see not teach thou me”. The negro don’t talk like this. “Surely it is meet to be said unto God, I have borne chastisement”: it is good to be able to say, I’ve been afflicted, I’ve been corrected. “I will not offend any more”: I’m sorry, I repent. “That which I see not teach thou me”: tell me about myself. “If I have done iniquity, I will do no more.”

That’s what it’s all about: growth. The adversity, the correction and the affliction are all to bring forth more growth in you.

“And he that hath knowledge will not grudge when he is reformed.” When you have the knowledge of the Lord, you are not going to grudge and bug out when you get reformed, meaning corrected, blasted, told about yourself, because all these things are to build us and refine us. We have to remember these things.

sense.text:
To refine is to remove impurities and unwanted elements, to improve something by small changes: to perfect, to hone, to temper, to fine-tune. Christ said be perfect; hone the fruits of the spirit; be temperate.

“Behold, I have refined thee”. God is refining us, honing us, fine-tuning us, making us perfect. “But not with silver”: silver gets put in actual fire. “I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction.” That is the purpose.

God is refining us so we don’t have to be in that lake of fire. We go through hell on this side so we don’t have to suffer on the other side. We have to choose which hell we want.

precepts.why:
“For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged.” Judging ourselves means examining ourselves and fixing our ways, keeping our bodies in subjection; then you don’t have to worry about man or God judging you.

“But when we are judged”, even by man, it is coming from the Lord, because all judgment is from the Lord. When we are corrected or demoted, “we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world.” Even in pain, suffering, demotion and correction, it’s all for our benefit, so you don’t have to die with Babylon. Jacked up, corrected, hot seat, blasted: God says all that is happening so you don’t get condemned with the world. Hell on this side or hell on the other side: take your pick.

“But the God of all grace, who hath called us unto his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after that ye have suffered a while”. Nobody said we wasn’t going to suffer. After that, he will “make you perfect”: refine you; “stablish”: you’re going to be rooted; “strengthen”; “settle you”: you are not going to be tossed to and fro or easily moved.

You will be stronger, and an example to those who come behind you. Everything has a purpose. We have many examples in the scriptures of our forefathers catching all manner of hell, but we skim right past them, thinking we are going to skate into the kingdom. We are not. Be not deceived.

sense.text: This is the apostle Paul speaking. “Howbeit whereinsoever any is bold, (I speak foolishly,) I am bold also.” How did he get this boldness, to the level in the spirit where he was willing to face death? Let’s see what he had to endure.

“Are they Hebrews? so am I. Are they Israelites? so am I. Are they the seed of Abraham? so am I.” He was “in stripes above measure”: able to take stripes beyond measure; “in prisons more frequent”: constantly thrown into prison; “in deaths oft”: constantly at an inch of death.

“Of the Jews five times received I forty stripes save one. Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned”: that was the stoning back in Acts 14; “thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep”.

“In perils by mine own countrymen”: that is other Israelites. “In perils among false brethren”: all that come in as Israel are not Israel. He caught all sorts of hell even from inside the body. “In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness.”

Besides all that, “the care of all the churches.” “Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is offended, and I burn not?” We have notable examples of our forefathers catching extreme levels of hell, and it made Paul bold, ready to take his death.

precepts.why:
A lot of Christians quote Philippians 4, I can do all things through Christ, but they don’t understand Paul’s resume. “For I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.” I have learned: stripes, beaten with rods, shipwreck, all those things.

“I know both how to be abased”: he had been abased many times and stayed in the spirit and kept fighting the fight, “and I know how to abound”. “Every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.” How do you know that if you never suffered adversity? You don’t know you until God tries you.

“I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.” Christians isolate that verse, but they don’t understand all it takes to get you to that spiritual level.

We have to remember our forefathers. Suffering is a spectrum, and the end of it is persecution and martyrdom; all these things are moulding us like the potter with the clay, to make us able to withstand.

“Take, my brethren, the prophets, who have spoken in the name of the Lord, for an example of suffering affliction, and of patience.” Look at the prophets of old.

Now examine Christ. “For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps”.

Look at his steps: he kept the laws, statutes and commandments, gathered his people, and then took his death. We have to do everything Christ did, all the way up until the end.

sense.text:
“We glory in tribulations also”. Brothers, are we on that level yet? We have to get to it. “Knowing that tribulation worketh patience”. All these spiritual level-ups come from suffering, adversity and tribulation. You don’t level up without going through it. Brothers say, I’m trying to grow in the spirit; from your mouth to God’s ears: oh, you want to grow? I got the perfect recipe.

You don’t get patience by everything going perfectly; what would you need patience for? You get it by building up that tolerance for suffering.

“And patience, experience”. Now when somebody else is going through it, you can give them counsel. Each one can teach one, and you’re not a hypocrite, because you actually went through it. You took your licks, took your stripes, went through the low. You went through a divorce and you stayed in this truth, ten toes down.

“And experience, hope”. What do you need hope for? Because there is more suffering to come; we ain’t seen nothing yet. So you build up your hope, which is faith.
“And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.”

precepts.why:
The times we are in bring all sorts of things: people in the hospital, people sick, a lot of tribulation and trials. Sometimes you would think the Lord has forsaken you and turned his back on you. A class like this helps you know you are not alone. The Lord has your back.

“Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb?” That is the question. “Yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.” When you go into that trial, when tribulation comes, when you say you can’t bear any more, the Lord says, yet will I not forget thee.

“Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands; thy walls are continually before me.” Each one of us is graven in the palm of his hand. We are never forgotten. Don’t let Satan put it in your mind that you are forgotten. The trial may feel too heavy, but the Lord has you, the same way he set Satan his limit with Job: don’t touch his life. The Lord is always around us, always protecting us. So never fear.

Become an example to everybody around you; but you have to endure it, and the Lord is with us. “Let us shew an example to our brethren, because their hearts depend upon us, and the sanctuary, and the house, and the altar, rest upon us.”

“Moreover let us give thanks to the Lord our God, which trieth us, even as he did our fathers.” We read about it: Job, Joseph, the prophets, Christ. “Remember what things he did to Abraham, and how he tried Isaac, and what happened to Jacob in Mesopotamia of Syria, when he kept the sheep of Laban his mother’s brother.”

“For he hath not tried us in the fire, as he did them, for the examination of their hearts”. He doesn’t even deal with us on those extreme levels; we ain’t ready yet. With all this knowledge, with Revelation broken down backwards, the Lord can’t yet try us the way he tried our fathers. “Neither hath he taken vengeance on us”.

“But the Lord doth scourge them that come near unto him, to admonish them.” Scourging is an instrument of torture. How many of us want to get closer to God? Not a hand went up. He scourges them that come near to him to admonish them, to refine us. So we can’t be moved by suffering, by sudden trouble, by fear or by death. The righteous, God’s elect, are going to still be standing when the smoke clears.

sense.text:
“But that on the good ground are they, which in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience.” This is the sincere part of the body. Having heard the word, they keep it: that’s application.

And they bring forth fruit with patience. What do you need patience for? Because even when you are doing the right things, suffering is part of the walk, family. We are constantly growing, constantly learning, constantly being moulded in the potter’s hands into a better product.

precepts.why:
“I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.” “Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away”: some spirits have to be taken away.

“And every branch that beareth fruit”: that’s the sincere, those who apply with patience, “he purgeth it”. To purge a tree is to prune it: carefully cutting back branches to control its size and shape and to revitalise the plant. The plant has to lose parts of itself to be revitalised. To purge an area can also mean to root out weeds and unwanted plants encroaching on a garden; sometimes the Lord has to purge you to remove what’s around you that ain’t good for you. The word comes from the Latin meaning to cleanse.

“That it may bring forth more fruit.” He has to cut branches off of you so you grow in the right size and grow properly in the spirit, and that don’t feel good. If you are sincere, everything is to make you better. Pain, obstacles, struggles, correction, demotion: the sincere will come out the other side of whatever calamity they face wiser, stronger, with more fruits of the spirit, their senses exercised. You won’t be the same person that walked into the storm; you always gain something in spite of what you consider a loss.

sense.text: “Cast not away therefore your confidence, which hath great recompence of reward.” Why would you cast away your confidence? Because you’re catching hell? We can’t cast it away by no means, no matter what we are going through. It is designed to teach you; it has purpose behind it. When the smoke clears, you get an increase in the spirit.

“For ye have need of patience”, and you ain’t getting that without adversity and suffering. “That, after ye have done the will of God, ye might receive the promise.” After you have done the will of God, against all odds, you are going to receive the promise.

precepts.why: “And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God”. That ain’t everybody. That’s the sincere, the good ground that brings forth fruit with patience: “to them who are the called according to his purpose.”

“And if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ”. It is a great glory to be a joint-heir with Christ, the Son of God: God can give us what he gave to his only begotten Son. “If so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together.”

Then you have to suffer everything, and the end of the rope is persecution; you have to suffer that too if it comes upon you. Not everybody is going to die, but some of us are going to go to jail. We have to be willing to suffer with Christ all the way to the end of that spectrum. There is no glory without suffering.

“For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.” Whatever we are facing on this side is nothing compared to it; it won’t even be spoken of in the kingdom. We have to meditate on our forefathers. The blueprint is right here.

“For which cause we faint not”. David said in Psalms 27 he would have fainted unless he believed to see the goodness of the Lord. “But though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.” God is constantly renewing us day by day, refining us, trying us.

“For our light affliction, which is but for a moment”: whatever you are going through, God calls that light affliction. Light work. It “worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory”.

“While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen”. What can we see today? Our people at the bottom, oppressed, the school-to-prison pipeline, our women whoring themselves out, our men sagging, drugging, thugging, killing, pimping. We don’t meditate on that. “For the things which are seen are temporal”: temporary. “But the things which are not seen are eternal”: us in glory, in rulership, in our proper place as kings on the earth. That’s why Hebrews says don’t cast away your confidence, which hath great recompence of reward.

sense.text: We have to endure whatever comes to us and learn what God wants us to learn from it to get the increase, and you don’t get the increase without enduring and applying what the Bible says. “Whosoever cometh to me, and heareth my sayings, and doeth them”: you have to apply, family. You have to apply, Israel. “I will shew you to whom he is like”: the one who comes into the truth and applies.

“He is like a man which built an house”: in Luke 14 it was called a tower. “And digged deep”: we dig deep by studying, learning and applying. “And laid the foundation on a rock”: the rock is Christ. Your foundation cannot be man; man will always disappoint you. Your foundation must be Christ.

“And when the flood arose”: pain, suffering, trials and hardship are going to come. It’s not an if, it’s a when. “The stream beat vehemently upon that house”: various and manifold temptations, upon you, your walk, your spirit, “and could not shake it: for it was founded upon a rock.” We can’t be moved, brothers and sisters. If that’s you and you are sincere, when this smoke clears you are going to be still standing.

precepts.why:
The rock is Christ. “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation”. Christ is our stone, that precious tried stone.

“He that believeth shall not make haste.” He that believes in Christ, no matter what happens, is not going to make haste. He is rooted.
